title: Haggard Wife
logline: A worn-down young wife is openly discarded by her husband for an older, wealthy mistress who funds his vices — until it surfaces that the wife comes from a powerful clan, and she quietly turns the humiliation back on both of them.

production_rules.location_ref_sourcing: A location reference must ALWAYS be an empty room/set with NO characters in it, generated fresh via Krea 2 — never extracted from an actual clip frame, even a clean-looking one. A frame with real characters in it (even partially, even just an arm at the edge) gives the model ambiguous body information alongside the two clean character portraits, and that ambiguity can hallucinate a phantom third person into the shot AND propagate through every later chained clip via last-frame conditioning (confirmed failure: Episode 1 Scene 1's first redo used a real clip-1 frame as the bedroom reference, which introduced a stray extra arm that then persisted through every subsequent clip in the chain). To get the details right without using a real frame: describe the specific established details (wall treatment, furniture, fixtures) explicitly in the Krea 2 prompt, generate it, and only then confirm it matches before use — do not reuse an in-scene frame as a shortcut.
production_rules.default_clip_length: VARIABLE per clip based on what that beat actually needs (starting Scene 2 onward — Scene 1 used a fixed 8s/192 frames throughout and that's fine as-is, not worth a redo just for this). h3's frame validation snaps to steps of 17 frames (~0.7s) apart — valid durations roughly every 0.7s from ~1s up to ~15s (e.g. 124=~5.2s, 175=~7.3s, 192=~8.0s, 226=~9.4s, 243=~10.1s). Pick shorter for a quick exchange, longer for a beat with an in-clip [Shot N] cut that needs room to breathe. Note shorter clips are ALSO more compute-efficient per second of footage (~4.25 min/sec at 8s vs ~5+ min/sec at 10-14s), so varying duration down when a beat is quick saves time too, not just a quality tradeoff.
production_rules.camera_variety_is_independent_of_clip_co: Varying camera angle per clip (close-up, reverse angle, pull-back, etc.) does NOT reduce how many clips a scene needs — clip count is set by h3's hard ~14.4s-per-generation ceiling (60s scene needs ~5 minimum regardless of framing style). Camera variety is a quality upgrade layered on top, not a way to cut clip count.
production_rules.no_last_frame_chaining_for_refs_mode: ROOT CAUSE FOUND AND FIXED for the recurring overexposed/grainy/streaky degradation that hit Scene 1 twice (once pre-format-fix, once again post-format-fix on clip 3 of the properly-formatted run). Cause: /api/sequence's automatic last-frame-folding adds each completed clip's actual output frame as an extra 4th reference for the next clip — any small artifact from one generation gets baked in and fed forward, compounding worse each clip (clip 1 clean, clip 2 a faint mark, clip 3 a visible reddish streak + grain). Confirmed fix by direct A/B test: generating the same clip independently via /api/generate (mode=refs) using ONLY the 3 fixed standing refs (character x2 + location), with NO first_frame/last_frame at all, came out completely clean. Standing references already anchor identity/scene consistency, so the pixel-exact last-frame handoff was never actually needed once refs-mode was in play — it was pure downside. RULE: never use /api/sequence's chaining for refs-mode clips going forward. Submit every clip independently via /api/generate with the same fixed refs list, wait for each to finish, then manually ffmpeg-concat all the clip files into the final scene at the end (no automatic merge, since /api/sequence is what does the chaining we're avoiding). GOTCHA: give each independently-submitted clip a UNIQUE seed. The server names each output file from a same-second timestamp + seed, so submitting several /api/generate calls back-to-back in a script with an identical fixed seed collides on the exact same output filename and each clip silently overwrites the previous one's file. Vary the seed per clip (e.g. base_seed + clip_index) even though refs-mode identity comes from the standing references, not the seed.
production_rules.prompt_format: STANDARD (confirmed working, use for every clip going forward): the official MiniMax H3 'Full-Reference Mode' six-section structure, not the plain filipino-ragebait-skill H3 template. See https://github.com/MiniMax-AI/MiniMax-H3/blob/main/skills/h3-prompt-writing/references/ref-en.txt for the source doc. Sections in order: (1) subject_definitions — <Subject 1>/<Subject 2> for characters, each citing their <Picture N> for identity inline; a standalone <Picture N> (not wrapped in a Subject) for the location/composition-only reference. (2) summary — '[reference generation] ' + one paragraph. (3) retention_analysis — state fully_preserved for each Subject's face/hair/body from its Picture, and clarify the location Picture contributes room/composition only, no characters. (4) detailed_description — the audio/dialogue-preservation critical-rules text, then one or more '[Shot N]' blocks; [Shot 1] has no timestamp, every later shot in the SAME clip is '[Shot N] At MM:SS.mmm, cut to ...' — this is a REAL in-clip camera cut, confirmed working (verified: wide two-shot at 0s cut to a genuine close-up at 4s within one 8s generation, clean identity, no artifacts). (5) overall_soundscape. (6) non_diegetic_music. This replaced three earlier failed attempts at getting camera variety via a trailing 'Camera: ...' sentence in the old template, which the model simply ignored.
production_rules.why_earlier_camera_attempts_failed: Two compounding causes, now both fixed: (1) the flawed bedroom reference (see location_ref_sourcing) was corrupting identity generally, which may have suppressed the model following ANY secondary instruction including camera direction; (2) the 'Camera: <description>' trailing-sentence approach was never the right mechanism at all — real camera cuts need the [Shot N] At MM:SS.mmm structure inside detailed_description, which is a different part of the prompt entirely. Don't reintroduce the old template even for clips that don't need an in-clip cut; use prompt_format for every clip for consistency.

clothing_drift_across_clips.issue: Marco's outfit drifted from a fitted crew-neck white undershirt (clips 1-3, ref image) to a looser sleeveless muscle tank in clip 4 (seed 100505), despite retention_analysis claiming clothing is scene-specific and body/face fully_preserved.
clothing_drift_across_clips.severity: minor - accepted, identity/face stayed clean, not worth a redo
clothing_drift_across_clips.lesson: retention_analysis alone does not lock garment style tightly enough across independently-generated refs-mode clips. Spell out exact garment details (fit, sleeve length, neckline, fabric) explicitly in every single clip's subject_definitions block, not just once loosely - do not rely on the ref image or a vague scene-clothing note to hold it steady clip-to-clip.
clothing_drift_across_clips.how_to_apply: From Scene 2 onward, repeat the full precise clothing description (not just "his usual outfit") in subject_definitions for every clip, same as face/hair/body details already are.

tagalog_pronoun_accuracy.lesson: amin (exclusive we/us, excludes listener) vs atin (inclusive we/us, includes listener) matters for accuracy - when a line is about the relationship between speaker and the person being spoken to ("there is no more us"), use atin, not amin.
tagalog_pronoun_accuracy.how_to_apply: Before finalizing any Tagalog dialogue with pronoun choices (amin/atin, kami/tayo, etc.), double check inclusivity/exclusivity matches who is actually being referred to.

phantom_duplicate_of_named_subject.issue: A named Subject can occasionally get cloned into a second copy of itself mid-clip (not just an unrelated stray limb like the earlier bedroom incident) - here Tatay Lino appeared twice simultaneously.
phantom_duplicate_of_named_subject.lesson: The standard no-third-person retention_analysis line is not always enough; when a scene has exactly one instance of a background/staff-type character, explicitly state EXACTLY TWO PEOPLE TOTAL and explicitly forbid duplicating/cloning either named subject. UPDATE: reinforcing the retention_analysis text alone was NOT sufficient - it recurred on the retry with the same wide two-shot framing. Second attempt tightened the shot (close two-shot, minimal background depth/empty space) since a wide shot with visible open background around a gate seems to invite the model to hallucinate a second staff/guard figure, and added explicit denial of a security-guard/watchman trope specifically (the model may default to gate scenes needing 2 guards). ROOT CAUSE FOUND: it was never really about duplication language strength - staging a gate-opening/crossing action creates an ambiguous crossing direction (rendered backward as exiting, twice) AND an implied gate-operator role that got duplicated into a second figure (twice, across two different framings/seeds). Fix: avoid staging the gate-crossing moment itself - stage the scene already past the threshold, gate closed and only in background, characters simply walking toward the house. Removing the ambiguous action fixed both bugs at once rather than needing ever-stronger denial language.
phantom_duplicate_of_named_subject.how_to_apply: Add this stronger anti-duplication phrasing by default for any future clip introducing a new, less-established minor character, especially in a two-shot with more open background space (like an outdoor gate scene) where a clone has room to render.

pacing_and_characterization_feedback.feedback_received: Early single-viewer review after Ep1 Scenes 1-2: (1) story drags, too much repeated context, wealth reveal (Scene 3) feels stretched; (2) the "haggard wife" premise from the title is never actually established - the conflict reads as generic cheating, not tied to her being run ragged from sacrifice/overwork; (3) why Marco specifically prefers Selina is never given texture beyond "she has money" - no sense of what she gives him emotionally (ego, admiration, ease) vs. what Teresas exhaustion costs the relationship.
pacing_and_characterization_feedback.action_taken: Re-cut (not regenerated) Scenes 1-2 to remove purely-repetitive clips, addressing complaint (1) only, since footage already existed. Complaints (2) and (3) require NEW footage/lines and could not be fixed by re-cutting alone.
pacing_and_characterization_feedback.how_to_apply_going_forward: Starting Scene 3 and into Episode 2-3: (a) every clip must reveal something the audience did not already know - if a clip only restates an emotional beat already landed, cut it before generating, not after; (b) explicitly establish the "haggard" premise with a concrete visual/line tying her exhaustion to sacrifice for the family (e.g. she works nights/second job, gave up her own plans, physically depleted from providing) rather than leaving it as an unexplained adjective; (c) give Marco a real, specific reason he prefers Selina beyond money - what she makes him FEEL (admired, like a man, unpressured) contrasted with what Teresas exhaustion/nagging-about-bills costs him emotionally, so the choice reads as a person, not a cliche.

scene_transition_bridging.lesson: A hard cut between two very different spaces (outdoor walkway with a companion -> alone indoors) reads as confusing/abrupt without any bridging action, even if narratively the audience can infer time has passed.
scene_transition_bridging.how_to_apply: When a scene moves from one location/character-configuration to another, give the new clip a brief opening beat (a few seconds) showing the character arriving/entering the new space, rather than starting already static/mid-activity in it - costs little runtime but preserves spatial continuity.

no_dragging_explosive_pacing.rule: Every scene must feel explosive - reveal after reveal, twist after twist - never a scene that just sits in one emotional beat restating itself. At the same time, speed must never come at the cost of clarity: the intent behind every line, the actual argument being had, and the WHY behind each character's choice must stay obvious to the viewer even at a fast pace.
no_dragging_explosive_pacing.why: User has no luxury of viewer patience - short-form drama lives or dies on immediate engagement. The goal is hook after hook so viewers watch the entire video, and a real emotional trigger landing every time, not passive viewing.
no_dragging_explosive_pacing.how_to_apply: Before writing a scene: list what NEW information/reveal each clip adds. If a clip does not add a new fact, twist, or escalation beyond the previous clip, cut it before generating (do not write it and trim later). Every scene should answer intent/argument/why clearly even as it moves fast - clarity and speed are not in tension, a well-written escalating scene achieves both. This supersedes any instinct to let a scene breathe or linger for atmosphere.

direction_ambiguity_root_cause.issue: Entering/exiting direction confusion recurred a 3rd time (gate clips 1/2, then this porch clip) even after removing the gate-crossing action specifically - the walking motion ITSELF (toward or away from camera) seems unreliable for the model to render with a clear/consistent direction.
direction_ambiguity_root_cause.fix_that_worked: Remove ALL walking motion from the clip - stage both characters already stationary in their final positions, with explicit body-orientation language (Teresa's front facing the house/door, never her back) instead of relying on motion direction to convey arrival.
direction_ambiguity_root_cause.how_to_apply: For any future clip where entering/arriving/approaching needs to be conveyed, default to a static already-arrived staging with explicit facing/orientation language, rather than depicting the walking motion itself.

first_frame_location_lock.issue: A clip can render its OPENING second or two in a completely unrelated location before correcting to the intended scene, even when the scene/staging is otherwise correctly described.
first_frame_location_lock.fix: Explicitly anchor the very first frame with language like 'From the very first frame, the camera is already on/in [LOCATION]...' and state 'there is no other location shown at any point in this clip' - don't just describe the final staging and assume the opening frame will match it.
first_frame_location_lock.how_to_apply: Apply this opening-frame anchor by default for any clip using a still/static staging (no walking-in motion establishing the location), since without that motion there's apparently nothing else pinning the model to the right location at frame one.

visual_artifacts_and_color_bleed.issue: A clip can render a persistent diagonal RGB-fringed streak artifact across frame, and a character's solid-color garment can drift to match a nearby character's different-colored garment mid-clip (Marco's navy shirt drifting to Selina's teal-green).
visual_artifacts_and_color_bleed.fix: Reroll with a new seed - this looks like a per-generation rendering quality issue, not something the original prompt did wrong. Reinforce with explicit language distinguishing the two garment colors ('never green, never teal' for the navy shirt) and a general 'no visual artifacts or streaks anywhere in frame' line as a preventive measure.
visual_artifacts_and_color_bleed.how_to_apply: Add this checks to the phantom-character/clothing-drift visual QA pass: also scan for (a) any persistent line/streak artifacts, (b) one character's colors bleeding into another's garment, especially with two characters in similar fabric (both wearing silk/satin in this case).

clip_to_clip_topic_bridging.issue: Even within one scene/location, consecutive clips written as separate self-contained beats can read as an incoherent topic jump if nothing in the first clip's ending motivates the next clip's opening topic.
clip_to_clip_topic_bridging.fix: End a clip with a concrete, visible/audible hook (a phone buzzing, someone entering, a specific line that raises the next topic) that the following clip's opening beat directly picks up - not just cutting to a new subject cold.
clip_to_clip_topic_bridging.how_to_apply: When writing multi-clip scenes, check the LAST beat of clip N against the FIRST beat of clip N+1 - if there's no causal or referential link between them, add one (even a small one like a phone buzzing) rather than relying on scene continuity alone to justify the jump.

reveal_causality_precision.lesson: When writing a reveal that connects a protagonist's family/company to an antagonist's wrongdoing, be precise about the DIRECTION of the financial/causal relationship - 'the corrupt money comes FROM our company' and 'they depend ON financing FROM our company' sound similar but imply opposite moral positions (source of corruption vs. leverage over someone else's corruption).
reveal_causality_precision.how_to_apply: Before finalizing any reveal dialogue involving money/company relationships between a sympathetic and unsympathetic character, explicitly check which direction responsibility/leverage actually flows, since a single preposition swap can accidentally implicate the wrong party.

no_burned_in_captions.issue: A clip can spontaneously render on-screen subtitle/caption text overlaying the dialogue at the bottom of frame, even though nothing in the prompt asked for it - likely the model's training data includes captioned video.
no_burned_in_captions.fix: Add an explicit CRITICAL VISUAL RULE denying subtitles/captions/text overlays/burned-in text, alongside the existing audio rules, as a standing part of every clip's prompt going forward (not just when it happens to show up).
no_burned_in_captions.how_to_apply: Add this line to the shared AUDIO_RULES/template block for every future scene's submission script by default, not just as a reactive fix - captions were not in the phantom-character/clothing-drift QA checklist before, add it as a standard visual QA check too.

framing_language_precision.issue: Vague emotional framing language like 'tight intimate two-shot' can get interpreted as an extreme close-up crop that loses the location entirely, rather than the intended warm-but-still-contextualized medium shot.
framing_language_precision.fix: Use concrete framing language instead of mood-only descriptors: 'medium two-shot... [location elements] clearly visible around them' rather than 'tight intimate.' Warmth/intimacy should come from acting direction (tone, expression) not from framing extremity, unless an actual close-up is specifically wanted.
framing_language_precision.how_to_apply: When writing shot descriptions, always pair any emotional/mood adjective (intimate, tense, warm) with an explicit framing type (medium two-shot, close-up, wide shot) and confirm the location stays visible unless a true close-up is intended. Also specify physical contact explicitly (or explicitly deny it) rather than leaving it to the model's interpretation, especially between characters with a formal/respectful relationship dynamic.

opening_shot_no_walking_for_retention.issue: Episode 1 posted with 73% retention at 5 seconds - a high early drop-off for content designed to hook immediately. Diagnosed cause: Scene 1 clip 1's opening actually shows Marco walking several seconds across the room toward Teresa before the confrontation visually starts, even though the scripted dialogue was timed to begin at 0.4s. The visual blocking (a 'walking into the room' beat) diluted the hook regardless of audio timing, and directly violates the drama skill's own explicit warning against opening on someone walking into a room.
opening_shot_no_walking_for_retention.fix: Stage every opening shot with both characters ALREADY in position - already close, already visibly tense - from the very first frame. No walking, no entering, no blocking that takes a few seconds to resolve into confrontation. This is the same fix as the direction_ambiguity_root_cause lesson (avoid walking motion in a clip), now confirmed to also matter for retention, not just direction-clarity.
opening_shot_no_walking_for_retention.how_to_apply: When writing any clip meant to open a video (not mid-scene continuation clips), explicitly describe the characters as already standing close/already facing each other/already mid-tension in the very first sentence of the shot description - never 'X walks toward Y' or 'X enters' as the opening action. Also worth checking (can't verify without audio): whether the AI-generated dialogue delivery timing matches the scripted second-by-second cues, since delivery pacing can drift from the script.
opening_shot_no_walking_for_retention.also_consider: Sound-off viewing is very common on social feeds (muted autoplay by default) - if the posted video has no burned-in caption/subtitle text, viewers who can't hear the hook line lose it entirely in the first few seconds. Worth testing a version WITH burned-in captions to see if retention improves, since this project's current convention is captions added separately in post rather than baked into generation.

weak_hook_vs_accusation.lesson: A hook line phrased as a neutral question ('Sino si Selina?' / 'Who is Selina?') doesn't carry inherent emotional charge - it reads as investigative curiosity, not accusation or hurt, until context is added. A hook line phrased as a raw, blunt STATEMENT OF FACT (especially a humiliating one, stated flatly rather than dramatically) hooks harder because it plants a question ('why/how did that happen?') without needing setup.
weak_hook_vs_accusation.example: Weak: 'Sino si Selina?' (investigative, no inherent charge). Strong: 'Pinagpalit ako ng asawa ko sa sugar mommy niya.' (a flat, humiliating statement of fact that immediately raises questions and carries built-in emotional weight).
weak_hook_vs_accusation.how_to_apply: When writing any opening/hook line, prefer a blunt declarative statement of a painful fact over a neutral question, especially when the audience doesn't yet have context - a statement forces curiosity ('what happened?') while a bare question can read as merely curious rather than urgent.

bedroom.description: Plain cream walls, wall-mounted split-type AC unit, sheer white curtains, dark wooden window frame, wooden dresser with mirror and warm bedside lamp, small framed picture on the wall, bed with floral-pattern sheets.
bedroom.note: Empty-room synthetic Krea 2 generation (outputs/gui-image-20260920-165657-seed1447222512.jpeg), no characters in it, matches all established details. Superseded two earlier bad attempts: (1) a synthetic image with wrong details (wallpaper instead of plain walls, no AC unit, wrong bedding), (2) a real extracted clip-1 frame that matched details but contained Teresa/Marco's actual bodies, which caused a phantom extra arm to appear and propagate through the whole chained scene. See production_rules.location_ref_sourcing.

gate.description: Exterior gate of Teresa's real home: plain grey concrete perimeter wall, simple steel gate, unremarkable/modest from outside on purpose, single warm porch light, dusk.

porch.description: Front porch of Teresa's real home, taken just outside the open front door. Door open, revealing an opulent interior beyond: crystal chandelier, marble floor, elegant curved staircase, warm gold lighting - deliberate contrast to the modest street-side gate. Porch itself stays understated/plain.

condo.description: Marco and Selina's upgraded high-rise condo, living room: floor-to-ceiling windows with city skyline view, curved white sofa, crystal pendant light, marble accent wall - deliberate contrast to the modest bedroom of Episode 1.

office.description: Teresa's private home office/study: large dark wood executive desk, tall bookshelf, deep green leather chair, warm brass desk lamp, old-money decor conveying quiet authority - where she conducts business and is visibly obeyed.

boardroom.description: An imposing corporate boardroom: long polished dark wood table, tall leather chairs, floor-to-ceiling windows with city skyline at night - where Teresa reveals herself to Selina.
boardroom.note: Two reference angles: boardroom-ref.jpeg (window end) and boardroom-door-ref.jpeg (entrance end, double doors) - use both together for clips involving someone entering through the door.

Teresa.description: TERESA is a 25-year-old Filipina woman, naturally beautiful but haggard from years of overwork, faint under-eye circles, dark hair usually pulled back into a low ponytail with loose strands, fine delicate features and high cheekbones still visible beneath the exhaustion. Early scenes: simple worn cotton house clothes. Later scenes (post-reveal): composed, elegant, understated wealth.

Marco.description: MARCO is a 25-year-old handsome Filipino man, short dark hair, clean-shaven sharp jawline, confident easy charming smile, warm brown eyes. Dresses well but not flashy early on; increasingly flashy/borrowed-glamour clothing as Selina funds his vices.

Selina.description: SELINA is a 42-year-old striking, confident Filipina woman, glossy dark wavy hair, bold red lipstick, refined makeup, dresses in expensive silk/satin blouses and gold jewelry. Poised, composed, seductive, used to getting her way.

Staff.description: A composed Filipino man in his 50s, neatly combed grey-streaked hair, clean-shaven, wearing a simple white long-sleeve barong-style shirt, calm and deeply respectful demeanor.

Maid.description: A Filipina woman in her mid-30s, neat black hair in a low bun, warm and welcoming expression, wearing a simple pale blue collared house-uniform blouse.

scenes.cliffhanger: Marco says he's not sorry, and that he's not ending it.

scenes.cliffhanger: A phone call: someone addresses her by a family name that clearly commands respect. She simply says, ‘Let them have their happiness. For now.’
